lead: This unit ties RF building blocks into a working radio: passive parts, noise and distortion, receiver and transmitter chains, LNAs, mixers, power amplifiers, oscillators and synthesizers. After it, you can read a transceiver block diagram, budget noise and linearity, choose an architecture, and explain the main exam specifications with numbers.
about: The unit builds a radio from its parts. 5.1 starts with on-chip inductors, capacitors and varactors, because loss and tuning set later limits. 5.2 adds noise figure, cascaded noise and sensitivity; 5.3 adds gain compression, intermodulation, IIP3 and dynamic range, so noise and distortion meet in the same budget. 5.4 and 5.5 use those budgets to compare superheterodyne, direct-conversion, image-reject receivers and transmitter/transceiver chains. 5.6, 5.7 and 5.8 then go inside the LNA, mixer and power amplifier: matching, conversion, classes, efficiency and linearization. 5.9 closes the loop with oscillators, VCO phase noise and frequency synthesizers, the local source every mixer needs. The order moves from component to specification to architecture to circuit, with each chapter using the numbers fixed earlier.

chapters.idea: Passive RF parts are not ideal; their loss, parasitics and tuning range decide noise, matching and frequency control.
chapters.depth: Cover on-chip spiral inductors: inductance, series resistance, shunt capacitance, Q factor, self-resonance, skin effect. Cover MIM and MOS capacitors: series resistance and inductance, Q. Cover varactor diode and MOS varactor: voltage-dependent capacitance C(V), tuning range, Q, and control-line noise. Some syllabi call Q the quality factor and varactors voltage-variable capacitors. Mention MMIC passives only as a one-line link to Unit 4. Keep field theory and S-parameters out.

figure.aria: RF passive families branch into inductor, capacitor and varactor, with their main parasitic or tuning notes.

chapters.example: A 2 nH spiral inductor at 2 GHz has series resistance 4 Ω and shunt capacitance 1 pF. Find its Q and equivalent parallel resistance. Also find its self-resonant frequency. ω = 2π × 2×10⁹ = 1.257×10¹⁰ rad/s. Q = ωL/R = (1.257×10¹⁰ × 2×10⁻⁹)/4 = 6.28. Rₚ ≈ Q²R = 39.4 × 4 = 158 Ω. f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π√(2×10⁻⁹ × 1×10⁻¹²)) = 3.56 GHz, so 2 GHz is below self-resonance.
chapters.trap: Using the ideal formula C = 1/(2πfX) and forgetting self-resonance; Q also changes with frequency, so one Q value is not valid over a wide band.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for microstrip and transmission-line parasitics; Unit 4 for microwave integrated circuits.
chapters.leave: S-parameters, couplers and power dividers to Unit 4; detailed impedance matching to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Noise figure measures SNR degradation; cascaded noise is dominated by the first stage, and sensitivity is the weakest signal for a required SNR.
chapters.depth: Define noise factor F, noise figure NF = 10 log₁₀F, noise temperature Te = (F − 1)T₀ with T₀ = 290 K. Cover Friis cascade F = F₁ + (F₂ − 1)/G₁ + (F₃ − 1)/(G₁G₂) + ..., with gains as linear power ratios. Cover sensitivity Pmin = −174 dBm/Hz + 10 log₁₀B + NF + SNRmin, where B is channel bandwidth in Hz. Refresh dB, dBm, voltage gain and channel. Define adjacent-channel rejection ACR and alternate-channel rejection AACR only as filter selectivity numbers, one line each. Keep intermodulation to 5.3.

figure.aria: A source drives an LNA, then a mixer, then an IF amplifier, with gain and noise figure values used in the cascade calculation.

chapters.example: An LNA has G₁ = 15 dB and F₁ = 2 dB. A mixer has G₂ = 10 dB and F₂ = 12 dB. An IF amplifier has G₃ = 20 dB and F₃ = 10 dB. Find the cascaded noise figure and the sensitivity for B = 10 MHz and required SNR = 10 dB. Use linear values: F₁ = 1.585, G₁ = 31.62, F₂ = 15.85, G₂ = 10, F₃ = 10, G₃ = 100. F = 1.585 + (15.85 − 1)/31.62 + (10 − 1)/(31.62 × 10) = 2.083. NF = 10 log₁₀(2.083) = 3.19 dB. Pmin = −174 + 10 log₁₀(10⁷) + 3.19 + 10 = −90.8 dBm.
chapters.trap: Adding NF values in dB directly, and using gain in dB in the Friis formula instead of converting to a linear power ratio.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 for the Friis link budget and dB; basic thermal noise.
chapters.leave: Gain compression and IIP3 to 5.3; receiver architecture choices to 5.4.

chapters.idea: Real amplifiers are nonlinear; compression and intermodulation set the largest tolerable signal and the dynamic range between noise and distortion.
chapters.depth: Cover AM-AM gain compression, 1 dB compression point P1dB,in and P1dB,out, two-tone third-order intermodulation IM3, input and output intercept points IIP3 and OIP3, and the 3:1 versus 1:1 slope rule. Define spurious-free dynamic range SFDR from the noise floor to the IM3 level. Cover blocking, dBc and spectral mask. Some syllabi write P1dBc for compression; use P1dB,in and P1dB,out to avoid confusion. Keep mixer-specific spurs to 5.7 and PA linearization to 5.8.

figure.aria: Output power versus input power: the ideal straight line and a measured curve that bends near compression, with input and output intercept values marked by the example numbers.

chapters.example: An amplifier has small-signal gain 20 dB, OIP3 = 30 dBm and P1dB,out = 20 dBm. Two input tones are each −10 dBm. Find IIP3, the ideal output per tone, the IM3 output level and P1dB,in. IIP3 = OIP3 − G = 30 − 20 = 10 dBm. Ideal output per tone = −10 + 20 = 10 dBm. IM3 output = 3 × 10 − 2 × 30 = −30 dBm. P1dB,in = 20 − 20 = 0 dBm.
chapters.trap: Treating IIP3 as a safe maximum input power; it is an extrapolated intercept and usually lies above P1dB by about 10 dB.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 for noise floor and sensitivity; dB and dBm from Unit 2.
chapters.leave: Mixer IIP3 and spurs to 5.7; PA back-off and predistortion to 5.8.

chapters.idea: Receiver architecture chooses where filtering, gain and frequency translation happen; superheterodyne, direct conversion and image reject trade image, DC offset and selectivity.
chapters.depth: Cover superheterodyne receiver: RF filter, LNA, mixer, IF filter, IF amplifier, demodulator. Define image frequency and high-side versus low-side LO. Cover direct conversion zero-IF: DC offset, flicker noise, IQ mismatch, even-order distortion. Cover image-reject mixing: Hartley and Weaver; only a few universities teach Weaver detail. Define image-reject ratio. Some syllabi call direct conversion zero-IF. Keep mixer internals to 5.7 and synthesizer to 5.9.

figure.aria: A superheterodyne receiver chain from antenna through RF filter, LNA, mixer, IF filter, IF amplifier and demodulator, with a local oscillator driving the mixer.

chapters.example: A superheterodyne receiver takes 900 MHz with IF = 45 MHz and a high-side LO. Find the LO and image frequency. A −20 dBm image blocker meets an RF filter with 30 dB rejection at the image, while the wanted signal is −80 dBm. Find the blocker power after the filter. LO = 900 + 45 = 945 MHz. Image = LO + IF = 945 + 45 = 990 MHz, or 900 + 2 × 45 = 990 MHz. Blocker after filter = −20 − 30 = −50 dBm, still 30 dB above the −80 dBm wanted signal.
chapters.trap: Placing the image at fLO − fIF for a high-side LO; the image spacing is 2fIF, and high-side and low-side LOs put it on different sides.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 noise and 5.3 blockers; Unit 2 for radio bands.
chapters.leave: Mixer conversion gain and spurs to 5.7; LO phase noise and synthesis to 5.9.

chapters.idea: A transmitter mirrors the receiver but power and spectral mask dominate; a transceiver shares LO, filters and duplexer.
chapters.depth: Cover direct upconversion transmitter: baseband, DAC, I/Q modulator, driver, PA, harmonic filter, duplexer or TDD switch, antenna. Cover two-step upconversion briefly. Define EIRP, ACLR and spectral mask. Cover shared LO and TX leakage into the receiver, duplexer loss, TDD switching. Some syllabi call ACLR adjacent-channel leakage ratio. Keep PA classes and efficiency to 5.8; keep modulator mixer detail to 5.7.

figure.aria: A direct-conversion transmitter chain from baseband through DAC, I/Q modulator, PA, duplexer and antenna, with a shared local oscillator feeding the modulator.

chapters.example: A direct-conversion transmitter gives 0 dBm at the modulator output. The PA has 25 dB gain and P1dB,out = 26 dBm. The filter and duplexer loss is 2 dB, and the antenna gain is 3 dBi. Find the EIRP and check PA compression. PA output = 0 + 25 = 25 dBm. EIRP = 25 − 2 + 3 = 26 dBm. The PA output is 1 dB below its 26 dBm P1dB,out, so compression is small but not zero.
chapters.trap: Multiplying dBm values or forgetting that duplexer loss applies to both TX and RX paths; EIRP is an add-and-subtract dB calculation.
chapters.prereq: 5.4 receiver chain; Unit 2 antenna gain and EIRP.
chapters.leave: PA classes, efficiency and linearization to 5.8; VCO and synthesizer to 5.9.

chapters.idea: An LNA must add little noise, enough gain, and stay linear and stable at the input of the receiver.
chapters.depth: Cover noise matching versus power matching, source degeneration inductor, cascode devices, gain, NF, IIP3, stability and bias. Compare BJT, MOSFET and HEMT only as LNA device choices; only a few universities teach HEMT detail. Cover input and output matching concepts, not full design. Some syllabi call this a low-noise amplifier. Keep mixer noise to 5.7 and PA to 5.8.

figure.aria: An LNA signal path from RF input through input matching, cascode device and output matching, with a bias block.

chapters.example: An LNA has gain 12 dB, NF = 1.5 dB, bandwidth 10 MHz, input P1dB = −10 dBm and IIP3 = 0 dBm. Find output P1dB, OIP3 and sensitivity for SNRmin = 10 dB. Output P1dB = −10 + 12 = 2 dBm. OIP3 = 0 + 12 = 12 dBm. Noise floor = −174 + 10 log₁₀(10⁷) = −104 dBm. Input-referred noise floor with NF = −104 + 1.5 = −102.5 dBm. Sensitivity = −102.5 + 10 = −92.5 dBm.
chapters.trap: Assuming minimum NF also gives minimum input reflection; the noise match and power match are different, and too much gain lowers overall linearity.
chapters.leave: Mixer noise and conversion to 5.7; power amplifier design to 5.8.

chapters.idea: A mixer multiplies RF and LO to shift frequency; conversion gain, noise, isolation and spurious products decide up-conversion and down-conversion.
chapters.depth: Cover mixer ports RF, LO and IF; passive and active mixers; conversion gain or loss; single-sideband and double-sideband noise figure; LO drive; isolation; 1 dB compression and IIP3; sum and difference products, image and LO leakage. Cover up-conversion and down-conversion with high-side and low-side LO. Some syllabi call a mixer a frequency translator. Keep oscillator phase noise to 5.9 and PA to 5.8.

figure.aria: A down-conversion mixer path from RF input through RF filter and mixer to IF filter and IF output, with the LO driving the mixer.

chapters.example: A down-converter receives RF = 2.45 GHz and uses IF = 100 MHz with a high-side LO. Find the LO and image frequency. The conversion gain is −6 dB. Find the IF output for an RF input of −20 dBm. LO = 2.45 + 0.10 = 2.55 GHz. Image = 2.55 + 0.10 = 2.65 GHz. IF output = −20 + (−6) = −26 dBm.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that a mixer produces both sum and difference frequencies; the unwanted one is the image and must be filtered before or rejected by the mixer.
chapters.leave: LO generation and phase noise to 5.9; PA drive level to 5.8.

chapters.idea: Power amplifiers trade efficiency against linearity; classes and linearization set output power, heat and spectral regrowth.
chapters.depth: Cover Class A, B, AB, C, D, E and F in one table of conduction angle, maximum drain efficiency and linearity. Define drain efficiency and PAE. Cover load line, matching, back-off, memory effects, digital predistortion, Doherty and envelope tracking at block level. Some syllabi call PAE power-added efficiency. Keep oscillator and synthesizer to 5.9; antenna and EIRP to Unit 2.

figure.aria: Drain efficiency versus output back-off for Class A and Class B, showing efficiency falling as the amplifier backs off from maximum power.

chapters.example: A Class AB PA has Vdd = 3.3 V, average current 300 mA, RF output 250 mW and RF input 50 mW. Find DC power, drain efficiency and PAE. PDC = 3.3 × 0.300 = 0.99 W. Drain efficiency = 0.250/0.99 = 25.3%. PAE = (0.250 − 0.050)/0.99 = 20.2%.
chapters.trap: Quoting peak efficiency at maximum output for a modulated signal; average efficiency at back-off is much lower, and PAE subtracts input RF power.
chapters.leave: Antenna gain and EIRP to Unit 2; oscillator noise to 5.9.

chapters.idea: An oscillator is a feedback loop with loop gain at least one and zero phase shift; phase noise and synthesizer loop bandwidth set spectral purity and tuning.
chapters.depth: Cover feedback and negative-resistance oscillator models, Barkhausen condition, LC and ring VCO, tuning range and KVCO, phase noise in dBc/Hz at an offset, Leeson shape with 1/f² and 1/f³ regions. Cover PLL blocks: phase-frequency detector, charge pump, loop filter, divider, reference; integer-N and fractional-N; lock time and spurs. Only a few universities teach fractional-N detail. Keep mixer operation to 5.7.

figure.aria: Phase noise versus offset frequency for a free-running VCO and a multiplied reference, using the example offset values.

chapters.example: A VCO at 2 GHz has phase noise −100 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset. A PLL multiplies a 10 MHz reference by N = 200. The reference phase noise is −150 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset. Estimate the multiplied reference phase noise and compare it with the VCO. Frequency multiplication adds 20 log₁₀N = 20 log₁₀200 = 46 dB. Multiplied reference = −150 + 46 = −104 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset. The reference path is 4 dB better than the free-running VCO at that offset.
chapters.trap: Treating dBc/Hz as total integrated phase noise; it is a density at one offset, and the PLL loop bandwidth decides which source dominates.
chapters.leave: Mixer conversion and spurs to 5.7; receiver and transmitter architecture to 5.4 and 5.5.
